section.title: The Cross Alone
section.sectionRationale: Paul takes the pen in his own hand to close the letter, and his final words gather up its whole message. The agitators want to boast in the flesh and avoid persecution for the cross; Paul will boast in nothing except the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him. What counts is not circumcision but a new creation. He blesses all who walk by this rule and bears on his body the marks of Jesus.
section.thesis: Everything in the letter comes to rest on the cross: the agitators seek to boast in the flesh and escape the cross's offense, but Paul boasts only in the cross of Christ, by which he is dead to the world, for what counts is not circumcision but the new creation, and grace and peace rest on all who live by this rule.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the true motives of the agitators, who compel circumcision to avoid persecution and to boast in the flesh; Paul's counter boast, only in the cross of Christ, through which the world is crucified to him and only new creation counts; and the closing blessing on all who walk by this rule, with the marks of Jesus and the grace of Christ.

units.label: The agitators' true motive
units.note: compelling circumcision to avoid the cross

verses.text: See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!
Those who want to make a good impression outwardly are trying to compel you to be circumcised. They only do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ.
For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves, yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.

units.label: Boasting only in the cross
units.note: the world crucified to me, a new creation

verses.text: But as for me, may I never {{kauchaomai|boast}}, except in the {{stauros|cross}} of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new {{ktisis|creation}}.

units.label: Peace on all who walk by this rule
units.note: the marks of Jesus and the grace of Christ

verses.text: Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God.
From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

kauchaomai.gloss: To boast, to glory in, to find one's confidence and pride in something. The agitators boast in the flesh, in numbers circumcised. Paul refuses every such boast and glories in one thing only, the cross of Christ. What a person boasts in reveals what they trust for their standing; Paul's whole hope and honor rest on Christ crucified, not on any achievement of his own.

stauros.gloss: Cross, the instrument of Roman execution and, for Paul, the center of the gospel. The cross is the one thing worth boasting in, for there Christ bore our curse and won our salvation. It is also the offense the agitators try to avoid, since a crucified Savior leaves no room for boasting in the flesh. Through the cross the world and Paul are dead to each other.

ktisis.gloss: Creation, that which is created; here new creation, the new reality God brings about in Christ. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision matters at all; what counts is that a person is made new by God's re-creating power. The gospel is not a religion of external marks but the dawn of the new creation, begun in those who belong to Christ and moving toward the renewal of all things.

basic.context: Paul takes the pen to write the ending himself, and he sums up everything. The agitators push circumcision to look good and to escape being persecuted for the cross. Paul wants to boast in only one thing, the cross of Christ, which has made him dead to the world and the world dead to him. Outward marks count for nothing; what matters is being a new creation. He blesses all who live by this and signs off with grace.
basic.hermeneutics: These are Paul's closing, summarizing words, written large in his own hand for emphasis. Read them as the point of the whole letter distilled: the cross alone, not the flesh, is the ground of boasting, and the gospel produces new creation, not new rule keeping.
basic.originalLanguages: The agitators kauchaomai, boast, in the flesh, but Paul boasts only in the stauros, the cross, of Christ. Through it the world is crucified to him. What counts is not circumcision but a new ktisis, creation, the new reality God makes in Christ.
basic.typology: The marks of Jesus that Paul bears, the scars of suffering for Christ, echo the sufferings of the servant and mark Paul as belonging to his crucified Lord. The new creation fulfills the prophetic promise of new heavens and a new earth, begun now in Christ and consummated at the end.
basic.christ: The cross of our Lord Jesus Christ is the center and climax of the letter. It is the one ground of boasting, the place where the world's power is broken, and the source of the new creation. Christ crucified saves, and to add circumcision is to flee the offense of His cross. The letter ends where it must, with grace from the Lord Jesus.
basic.god: God is the maker of the new creation, the one who re-creates people in Christ so that outward marks mean nothing. He grants peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule. The whole letter has defended the freeness of His grace, and it closes with that grace pronounced over the readers.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 1 says Paul preaches Christ crucified and boasts only in the Lord. 2 Corinthians 5 says anyone in Christ is a new creation. Philippians 3 counts all gain as loss for the sake of Christ.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible moves toward the cross and the new creation. Here Paul gathers both: he glories only in the cross, and he declares that what counts is being made new. The story that began in a broken creation ends in a new one, secured by Christ crucified and pronounced over all who live by this rule.

context.literary:
Galatians 6:11 to 18 is the postscript, and the shift is audible. Up to now Paul has been dictating, and the letter has moved through argument (chapters 1 and 2 on his own story, chapters 3 and 4 on Abraham, promise and law) and then exhortation (chapters 5 and 6 on freedom and the Spirit). Here the pen changes hands and the whole letter is compressed into a handful of sentences. Ancient letter writers often added a few closing words in their own hand to authenticate what a scribe had written, and Paul does the same at 1 Corinthians 16:21, Colossians 4:18 and 2 Thessalonians 3:17. What is unusual is that he calls attention to the size of the script.

The passage is built as a contrast. Verses 12 and 13 describe the opponents in three clauses, each with a motive: to look good, to avoid persecution, to boast in your flesh. Verses 14 to 16 answer them point for point. Where they boast in flesh, Paul boasts only in the cross. Where they count circumcision, Paul counts it as nothing, and says the same of uncircumcision. Where they are anxious about escaping the cross, Paul has been crucified to the world through it. Verse 17 then turns the persecution they dread into a badge he wears.

The section also closes loops. The 'new creation' of verse 15 answers the 'present evil age' of Galatians 1:4, the rescue the Lord Jesus accomplished at the start of the letter. The 'rule' of verse 16 gathers up the 'walk' language of Galatians 5:16 and 5:25. The benediction of verse 18 mirrors the opening wish of Galatians 1:3, so the letter begins and ends with grace, wrapped around a long defence of it. Notice the last word before 'Amen' is 'brothers', placed at the very end of the Greek sentence, a small touch of warmth after a letter that has often been stern.
context.historical:
Galatians was written to churches in the Roman province of Galatia, which Paul had founded, and the cause of the letter was a rival mission. Teachers had arrived after Paul left, insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to the people of God. Paul's own sketch of the visit to Jerusalem in Galatians 2:3 to 5 shows that the same pressure had come to a head before, when 'false brothers' tried to force circumcision on Titus, a Greek, and Paul refused to yield. Where the Galatian churches stood, and whether the letter is early or later in Paul's ministry, are matters scholars still discuss, but nothing in these closing verses depends on settling them.

The social pressure behind verse 12 is easy to miss. In the Roman world, Jews were generally tolerated in their ancestral customs, and circumcision marked a person as belonging to that recognised community. A Gentile Christian group that stood outside the synagogue and also refused civic cults could draw attention. Many readers suggest the agitators wanted the Galatians to look like a branch of Judaism so that they, and their Jewish Christian sponsors, could escape being targeted by zealous Jews who resented a law-free gospel. Paul had seen this zeal from the inside, since he had once been a persecutor himself, Galatians 1:13 and 1:23.

Paul's sentence about 'large letters' has a personal background as well. In Galatians 4:13 to 15 he recalls that he first preached to them because of an illness, and that they would have torn out their eyes and given them to him. Some have taken that as a hint of poor eyesight; the text does not say so, and it is safer to say only that he wrote bigger and bolder than a scribe would, for emphasis. The 'marks' of verse 17 are best read against the record. Acts 14:19 describes a stoning at Lystra, a Galatian city on any reading, and 2 Corinthians 11:23 to 25 lists lashings, rods, and a stoning. Paul's body carried the story of a man who had paid for his message.
context.canonical:
The closing of Galatians gathers threads from across the Old Testament and then points forward. Circumcision begins with Abraham, Genesis 17:10 to 14, as the sign of a covenant, and Paul has already argued that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, Romans 4:11. The law itself looked beyond the knife to the heart: 'The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts,' Deuteronomy 30:6, and Jeremiah 4:4 called Israel to circumcise the heart. When Paul says circumcision counts for nothing, he is not dismissing the Old Testament; he is saying its own promise of a changed heart has arrived.

The 'new creation' of verse 15 draws on Isaiah. 'Behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth,' Isaiah 65:17, and in the same breath God promises to create Jerusalem as a joy. Isaiah 43:18 and 19 says 'I am about to do something new.' Paul takes the long hope of a remade world and says it has already begun inside the old one, in the believer who belongs to Christ. The blessing of verse 16, 'peace and mercy,' echoes the benedictions of the Psalms, for example 'Peace be upon Israel,' Psalm 125:5, and Numbers 6:26.

The cross has its own Old Testament shadow. Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, and Paul has already used that text in Galatians 3:13 to say Christ 'became a curse for us.' So the thing the world counted shameful becomes the thing Paul boasts in.

Looking forward, the same boast is repeated in 1 Corinthians 2:2, 'Jesus Christ and Him crucified,' and Philippians 3:3 describes believers as those 'who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh.' The new creation is picked up in 2 Corinthians 5:17 and reaches its finish in Revelation 21:5, 'Behold, I make all things new.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Galatians to leave the letter holding one sentence: the cross is the only thing worth boasting about. Everything before this was an argument; here he asks for a decision. He does not simply tell them the opponents are wrong. He tells them why the opponents are doing it. Verse 12 and verse 13 are an uncovering of motives, so that the Galatians can see that the pressure to be circumcised has less to do with their good and more to do with the teachers' reputation and safety. A church that understands why it is being pushed is harder to push.

He also wants them to see what the choice costs and what it gives. It costs the comfortable approval of a religious community and may bring trouble, as it has for him. It gives belonging to a new creation, a family in which the old distinction of Jew and Gentile no longer sorts people, as he said in Galatians 3:28. The blessing of verse 16 is for those who 'walk by this rule', so he is also asking for a way of life, not just a creed. Finally, verse 17 is not a threat. It is a plea from someone who has bled for them to stop adding to his burdens and to trust the gospel he gave them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is Paul's description of himself and of his opponents, and the description is not automatically a command. The statement that he bears marks on his body is a record of what he suffered, not a call for believers to seek wounds or to measure faith by pain. Paul elsewhere says suffering comes to those who follow Christ, 2 Timothy 3:12, but he never tells anyone to chase it.

The prescriptive core is smaller and sharper: boast only in the cross (verse 14), count outward religious status as nothing (verse 15), and walk by the rule of the new creation (verse 16). These carry over directly. The specific sign at issue, circumcision, belonged to a covenant stage now fulfilled, but the habit underneath it, trusting visible badges for standing with God, survives in many forms: the right church, the right ritual, the right tribe, the right performance. The application is not that nothing outward matters, since Paul also wants love and good works, Galatians 5:6 and 6:10, but that none of it is the ground of acceptance or of pride.

debates.question: Who is 'the Israel of God' in verse 16?

views.label: The church of Jews and Gentiles together
views.case: The sentence says peace and mercy come on 'all who walk by this rule', and 'even to' can be read as 'that is, the Israel of God', defining the group by the rule. Paul has argued that those who have faith are sons of Abraham, Galatians 3:7, and that believers are Abraham's seed, Galatians 3:29. Romans 9:6 says that not all descended from Israel are Israel, and Philippians 3:3 says 'we are the circumcision.' Calvin and most of the Reformers read it this way.

views.label: Believing Jews within the church
views.case: Here the 'and' or 'even' sets two groups side by side: Gentile believers who walk by the rule, and Jewish believers who also do. Paul never uses 'Israel' of the church as a whole anywhere else, and Romans 9 to 11 keeps the word for ethnic Israel. Reading it this way keeps Paul from seeming to strip the name from his own people.

views.label: The people of Israel who will yet turn to Christ
views.case: Some take the phrase as a blessing prayed over the Jewish people as a whole, in line with Romans 11:25 and 26, where Paul expects 'all Israel' to be saved. The blessing is then a hope for their future, offered after the blessing on the Gentiles.

debates.bearing: The first view fits the letter's flow best, since the whole argument is that Abraham's family is defined by faith in Christ, but the second and third are held by careful readers and do not change the main point. On every reading, nobody is blessed by adding circumcision to Christ; the blessing falls on those who live by the new creation.

debates.question: What is the rule Paul speaks of in verse 16?

views.label: The statement of verses 14 and 15
views.case: The rule is the immediate sentence: the cross is the only boast and new creation is the only thing that counts. 'This rule' points back at what has just been said, and a rule in this sense is a measuring line against which a life is checked.

views.label: The whole gospel of grace taught in the letter
views.case: The rule is the principle of the entire letter, that justification and life come by faith in Christ and the Spirit, not by law keeping. The verbs for walking in Galatians 5:16 and 5:25 suggest a pattern of life that this standard shapes.

debates.bearing: Both fit because verse 15 compresses the letter. The practical bearing is the same: churches and believers are tested by whether their boast and their life line up with the crucified Christ, not by outward badges.

study.originalLanguages:
Four expressions in this short passage repay slow reading.

The first is Paul's phrase about the letters. In verse 11 he writes that you see how large letters he has written with his own hand. The Greek asks 'how large' in an exclamatory sense, and the verb is in the aorist, which can be read either as describing what he is writing now or as the epistolary aorist, describing the letter from the reader's point of view. The point is that the script is big and the message is urgent. It is the one place where the reader sees the apostle himself.

The second is the verb behind 'make a good impression', in verse 12. It is built on the Greek word for face, prosopon, and means to put on a good face, to look well in the flesh. It belongs to the vocabulary of appearance and of what people see. Paul sets it against the cross, which no one in the ancient world would have called good looking. The same section uses the present tense for 'are trying to compel', which means the agitators keep pressing, not that they did so once.

The third is the shape of verse 14, 'may I never boast.' The Greek uses the optative mood with a negative, the form translators often render 'God forbid.' Paul uses the same idiom in Romans 6:2 and Galatians 2:17, where he rejects an idea as unthinkable. Here it governs the boast: it is not that he declines to boast, it is that boasting in anything else is unthinkable. The verb 'has been crucified', used of both the world and himself, is in the perfect tense. It describes a completed event whose effect remains, so the cut between Paul and the world is permanent and not a passing mood. The relative phrase 'through which' can refer to the cross or to Christ, since both are masculine in Greek, and the sense is nearly the same.

The fourth is the word 'new' in 'new creation', verse 15. Paul uses kainos, which stresses new in kind or quality, not neos, which stresses new in time. The creation is not merely recent; it is different in character. Alongside it, the 'rule' in verse 16 is the Greek kanon, a measuring rod or standard, from which we get 'canon.' The verb for 'walk by this rule' is stoicheo, meaning to walk in line or step, the same verb used at Galatians 5:25, 'let us also keep in step with the Spirit.'

Last, 'marks' in verse 17 is stigmata, a word used for the brand marks that identified a slave or a devotee. Paul wears the brands of Jesus, the sign of whose slave he is. The translation 'marks of Jesus' does not tell us whether the genitive means marks that Jesus gave or marks that show whose he is, and both readings fit.

typology.type: Circumcision of the flesh to circumcision of the heart
typology.fulfillment: Circumcision was the sign of Abraham's covenant, Genesis 17:11, and it pointed past itself to a heart made new, Deuteronomy 30:6. Paul says that in Christ the pointing has arrived: 'In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ,' Colossians 2:11. The sign was a cut in the body; the fulfilment is a cut away of the old self at the cross, Galatians 5:24. The type falls short because it marked only male members of one nation and could not itself change the heart, as Jeremiah 9:25 and 26 warns.

typology.type: The one hung on a tree
typology.fulfillment: Deuteronomy 21:23 treated an executed man hung on a tree as under God's curse, and he was to be taken down by evening. Paul reads the cross through that text in Galatians 3:13: Christ 'became a curse for us.' The law's curse falls on the One who bore it, and the shame of the tree turns into the ground of the believer's blessing, as in 1 Peter 2:24. The type cannot show why the curse fell on an innocent man; that is what the cross adds, since He bore the curse in the place of others and not for His own sin.

typology.type: New heavens and new earth begun in the believer
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 65:17 promised a created newness reaching to the whole world, and Revelation 21:1 shows it arriving. Paul's phrase 'new creation' says the first part of that promise has landed in advance, in people. In 2 Corinthians 5:17 the same words describe anyone 'in Christ.' The pattern is already and not yet: the person is made new now, while the groaning creation still waits for its own release, Romans 8:19 to 22. It falls short of completeness until the body is raised and the earth itself renewed.

Isaiah 53:5 says of the servant, 'He was pierced for our transgressions,' and the wounds are the means of healing. Paul's scars are not saving, and he never says so, but he understands his body as a place where the pattern of Christ's suffering repeats, 2 Corinthians 4:10 and Colossians 1:24. The correspondence is witness, not atonement: Christ's wounds redeem, Paul's wounds show whom he serves. The type is thus limited, for no apostle's suffering adds to the finished work of the cross.

study.christ:
This passage does not lead to Christ through a hidden symbol; it puts the crucified Lord in the middle of the sentence. Yet there are several angles worth looking at.

First, by title. Paul writes 'our Lord Jesus Christ' in verse 14 and again at the very end, verse 18. The name is full: the Lord who rules, the one who saves, the anointed one of Israel's hope. The letter opened with 'the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age,' Galatians 1:3 and 1:4. The same Lord who began the letter's rescue now closes it.

Second, by the cross itself. The cross is what the opponents try to avoid and what Paul will not leave. 1 Corinthians 1:23 calls Christ crucified 'a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,' and Galatians 5:11 uses the phrase 'the offense of the cross.' To add circumcision to faith is to make the cross less offensive, because it adds a human contribution beside it. Paul's boast insists the cross is enough on its own. At the cross Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse, Galatians 3:13, and the message of the cross, which looks like foolishness to the perishing, is the power of God to those being saved, 1 Corinthians 1:18.

Third, by union. Paul says the world has been crucified to him through the cross. In Galatians 2:20 he said, 'I have been crucified with Christ,' and in 5:24 'those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh.' The cross is not only an event Christ went through for us; it is an event the believer is joined to. Romans 6:6 says our old self was crucified with Him.

Fourth, by new creation. Christ's resurrection is the first act of the new creation, and 'the firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18, is the head of the new humanity. Verse 15 is possible because the crucified One was raised. He is the second Adam, and the new creation is what a person is when joined to Him, 2 Corinthians 5:17.

Fifth, by presence. The letter ends with 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.' Grace is not a thing handed out apart from Him. It is His, and it comes as He comes. The marks Paul wears belong to Him as well: Paul says he carries around 'the death of Jesus,' 2 Corinthians 4:10, so that the life of Jesus would show in the same body.

We should guard against forced allegory. The 'large letters' do not secretly represent the cross, and the numbers of his scars are not symbols. Paul is simply, directly, pointing to Christ crucified as the only boast.
study.god:
This passage speaks of God more by what it assumes than by what it says, and what it assumes is large.

God is the maker of a new creation. 'What counts is a new creation' is not a phrase about human self-improvement. Creating is the work of God alone, as in Genesis 1 and Isaiah 65:17. The one who spoke the first world into being is now remaking people. This means salvation is not a repair of what we can fix ourselves, but a fresh act of the Creator, which is why no human achievement, including circumcision, could add to it.

God is the one who judges human boasting. Paul's whole line, 'may I never boast except in the cross,' assumes that boasting before God is the question of how we stand with Him. Jeremiah 9:23 and 24 says the one who boasts should boast in knowing the LORD, who practises kindness, justice and righteousness, and Paul has quoted that logic in 1 Corinthians 1:31. A God who is holy and gracious leaves no room for anyone to say 'I earned this', and leaves no reason for anyone to fear that they cannot.

God is the one who gives peace and mercy. These two gifts are placed in a deliberate order. Peace first, the end of hostility between the sinner and God, as in Romans 5:1, then mercy, the continuing compassion that keeps the believer. Both come to 'all' who walk by the rule. God's welcome is wide and has no ethnic ticket attached.

God is faithful to His people through suffering. Paul bears the marks of Jesus, and the God who allowed this is the same God who raised Jesus. Suffering in the service of the cross is not a sign of divine absence. It is the sign of a God who has Himself gone through the cross.

God is Trinitarian here. The Lord Jesus Christ is named twice; the Spirit has filled the letter from chapter 3 to chapter 5, Galatians 5:16 to 25; and the Father is 'our God and Father' of Galatians 1:4, whose will the Lord Jesus carried out. The letter ends with a prayer that the grace of the Lord Jesus go with the Galatians, which assumes Christ is present and able to give grace.

For worship, this means the right response is not self-congratulation but gratitude and quiet confidence. A God who makes a new creation and gives it as a gift is a God who is to be praised, not impressed.

crossReferences.note: Paul's earlier statement of union with Christ in the cross: 'I have been crucified with Christ.' Galatians 6:14 is the same truth seen from the outside, with the world as the thing that has died to him. The two verses bracket the argument of the letter.

Paul says that if he still preached circumcision, 'the offense of the cross has been abolished.' This explains the motive of verse 12, since adding circumcision removes the scandal of the cross and with it the persecution that scandal brings.

'In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. All that matters is faith, expressed through love.' This is the same claim as verse 15, but there the positive thing is faith working in love, here it is new creation. They describe one reality from two sides.

Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse, hung on a tree. This is why the cross is something to boast in rather than hide: what looked like a divine curse upon a criminal is the place where the curse on others was taken away.

'We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed.' It explains the marks of verse 17: suffering in the apostle's body is the place where the life of the risen Christ is shown to others.

'It is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh.' Paul redefines the people of God by the same boast and the same refusal of the flesh, close to Galatians 6:13 to 15.

Abraham 'received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.' This is the older root of Paul's claim that circumcision is not the ground of standing, and it lets the Galatians see that he is defending Abraham's own story.

'In Him you were also circumcised... with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands.' Paul speaks of a circumcision of the whole old self in Christ, which is the reality his boast in the cross pictures. It supplies what verse 15 means by saying that circumcision counts for nothing.

'Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel... it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring.' This bears on 'the Israel of God' in verse 16, showing that Paul can speak of a true Israel defined by promise, not descent alone.

'Behold, I make all things new.' The new creation Paul speaks of in verse 15 finds its full completion here, when what begins in believers now reaches the whole created order under the One on the throne.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a creation declared good and a humanity made to bear God's image, then tells how that creation was broken, Genesis 3. The long story that follows is God's rescue, and Galatians 6:11 to 18 stands near its hinge. The rescue Paul describes began in the promise to Abraham, Genesis 12:3, 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you', and the law came later as a guardian, Galatians 3:24. Circumcision was the sign of that first covenant. By the time Paul writes, the one the promise was about has come, been killed, and been raised. The sign that pointed ahead has been overtaken by the thing it pointed to.

What the passage answers from earlier in the story is the question of who belongs to God's people and on what terms. Israel was called out of the nations, yet the promise was always for the nations through Abraham's seed. If Christ is that seed, Galatians 3:16, then to belong to him is to belong to Abraham's family, and circumcision cannot be the gate. The cross removes the wall between Jew and Gentile, and Ephesians 2:14 to 16 shows how it makes the two into one new man.

What it sets up is a church that lives between the cross and the new heavens and earth. Believers are already a new creation, Galatians 6:15, but they still live in 'the present evil age,' Galatians 1:4, and the groaning creation still waits for liberation, Romans 8:19 to 22. The church's task is to walk by the rule of the new creation, to carry one another's burdens, Galatians 6:2, and to do good to everyone, 6:10. The cross is the means, the Spirit is the power, and the new creation is the shape.

How it ends: Revelation 21:5 has God say, 'Behold, I make all things new.' The marks that Paul bore will be gone, because there will be no more death or mourning or pain. The multiethnic people purchased by Christ's blood, Revelation 5:9, will stand together with no distinction that divides. And the cross, which now looks like weakness to the world, will be seen as the place where the new creation was won. Paul's single boast turns out to be the thing all creation will sing about at the last.

sermon.title: Boasting in the Cross (Galatians 6:11 to 18)
sermon.why: Keller brings the letter to its climax in the cross, showing why Paul boasts in nothing else, how the cross crucifies the world to the believer, and why the gospel produces new creation rather than boasting in the flesh.

quiz.q: Why were the agitators compelling the Galatians to be circumcised?

options.text: To make a good impression and avoid persecution for the cross.
options.note: Verse 12 exposes their self serving motive.

options.text: Out of sincere love for the Galatians' souls.
options.note: Paul says their motive was to avoid persecution and boast in the flesh.

options.text: Because they themselves kept the whole law perfectly.
options.note: Verse 13 says they did not even keep the law themselves.

options.text: Because God had commanded it for salvation.
options.note: The whole letter denies that circumcision is required for salvation.

quiz.q: In what does Paul say he will boast?

options.text: Only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: Verse 14 names the cross as his single boast.

options.text: In the number of converts he has made.
options.note: That is the agitators' boast in the flesh, not Paul's.

options.text: In his own record of law keeping.
options.note: Paul counts such things as nothing; he boasts in the cross.

options.text: In his sufferings as an achievement.
options.note: He bears the marks of Jesus, but his boast is the cross of Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul say truly counts?

options.text: A new creation, not circumcision or uncircumcision.
options.note: Verse 15 states the sum of the letter.

options.text: Being circumcised as a mark of belonging.
options.note: Circumcision means nothing; new creation is what counts.

options.text: Keeping the calendar of special days.
options.note: Outward observance does not count; new creation does.

options.text: Impressing others outwardly.
options.note: That is the agitators' aim, which Paul rejects.

quiz.q: What has the cross done, according to verse 14?

options.text: Through it the world has been crucified to Paul, and he to the world.
options.note: The cross breaks the world's hold on the believer.

options.text: It has made the law the way of salvation.
options.note: The cross ends boasting in the flesh, not establishes law as salvation.

options.text: It has left Paul still enslaved to the world.
options.note: The opposite; he is now dead to the world through the cross.

options.text: It has become a reason to boast in the flesh.
options.note: The cross removes all boasting in the flesh.

quiz.q: How does Paul end the letter?

options.text: With grace and peace on all who walk by this rule, and the grace of Christ.
options.note: Verses 16 and 18 close with blessing and grace.

options.text: With a final demand that they be circumcised.
options.note: He closes with grace, not a demand for circumcision.

options.text: With a curse on the whole church.
options.note: The curse was on those who distort the gospel; he blesses the faithful.

options.text: With a boast in his own accomplishments.
options.note: He boasts only in the cross and blesses them with grace.

questions: Paul boasts in nothing but the cross. Honestly, what are you most tempted to boast in or find your identity in, and how does the cross reframe it?
Through the cross the world was crucified to Paul. What hold does the world's approval still have on you, and what would being dead to it look like?
What counts is a new creation, not outward marks. Where are you tempted to measure your faith by externals rather than by God's re-creating work?
The agitators wanted to avoid the offense of the cross. Where are you tempted to soften the gospel to escape opposition or fit in?
The letter ends with grace be with your spirit. As you finish Galatians, how has the message of grace apart from works landed on your own heart?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes through which can also be rendered through whom; either way the cross of Christ is the means by which the world is crucified to Paul.
The Israel of God is most naturally read as all who walk by this rule, the believing community defined by faith in Christ, in keeping with the letter's argument about the true children of Abraham.
The marks of Jesus are the scars Paul bore from suffering for Christ, branding him as belonging to his Lord, in pointed contrast to the mark of circumcision.
